description: A header declaring `example-withdrawn-2026`, which the verifier's registry lists as `withdrawn`. Refused at §4 step 3, and refused for the **registry's** reason rather than a local one: §6 makes withdrawal binding on every deployment, so a verifier that continued to accept it would be the downgrade the registry exists to prevent. The internal reason separates it from a suite this deployment merely does not accept; the wire value does not, because the difference is the custodian's minimum acceptable policy.

notes: This registry is UNSIGNED, exactly as registry/manifest.json is. A verifier pins a signing key and a registry digest; neither exists yet, so no deployment may trust this file. P-003 open question 1 resolved that it is pinned the same way the predicate manifest is, and the predicate manifest's own signature is P-005's to build.

A file that decides which algorithms a verifier accepts is the last one that should be unauthenticated. That is why the pinning path is built now, with one entry, rather than retrofitted when a second suite makes it load-bearing.

This file proposes; the verifier decides. Presence here is not acceptance: a suite is used only if it is also in the verifier's own acceptable set, which is local configuration and is never derived from a message.
Suite identifiers are permanent. A registered identifier is never reused for different parameters, so a change in parameters is a new identifier rather than a new version of this one.

deprecated.why: Receipts signed under it remain evidence, so verification must continue. crypto-suites.md §6.

withdrawn.why: Continuing to accept it is the downgrade the registry exists to prevent. crypto-suites.md §6.

status_semantics.note: Recorded here for a reader; the rules themselves are crypto-suites.md §6's and are NOT data. An implementation reads each suite's `status` from this file and applies §6 to it — it does not read these three objects, and a registry that changed them would change nothing. That is deliberate: a registry able to redefine what `withdrawn` means could reinstate a suite it had withdrawn. Neither status retroactively invalidates a receipt: a verifier assessing an old one reads the suite it records and judges accordingly, which is only possible because the suite is recorded (crypto-suites.md §5).

suites.algorithm: Ed25519 (RFC 8032), with the acceptance rule in spec/crypto-suites.md §3
suites.serialization: JWS compact form (RFC 7515 §7.1) over a payload produced under spec/serialization.md §1
security_notes: The protected header carries exactly `suite` and `key_id` and no others. It is read before verification, so every member is a pre-authentication input surface.

No `alg` member. A Q2D signed string is therefore not a conformant JWS and JOSE tooling rejects it, which is the intended outcome: a header a general-purpose library can process is one where that library selects the verification algorithm from attacker-controlled data.
Which signatures verify is not left to the implementation's library. spec/crypto-suites.md §3 states four rules, and widely-used libraries sit on both sides of two of them.

suites.algorithm: none — an illustrative entry, not a registration
suites.serialization: none — an illustrative entry, not a registration
suites.hash: none — an illustrative entry, not a registration
security_notes: Registered by a vector, never by the project. It exists so a verifier's registry can be described as holding a suite with a status, which is the fact these vectors assert.
